summary:
Eiserion is an AI-powered astronaut bone-health management system designed to address one of the major challenges of long-duration spaceflight: microgravity-induced bone loss. Focusing particularly on vulnerable skeletal regions such as the hips, pelvis, spine, and lower limbs, Eiserion integrates bone-health monitoring through Quantitative Ultrasound (QUS), nutritional tracking, and exercise monitoring into a unified platform.

Its adaptive system connects nutrition and exercise through a two-way feedback loop: daily nutritional intake influences future exercise planning, while physical workload informs future nutritional estimates. AI analyzes the collected information, identifies trends, explains recommendations, and highlights potential concerns and uncertainties.

By combining bone-health measurements with nutritional and physical activity data, Eiserion aims to support more informed, personalized astronaut health management and contribute to protecting skeletal health during extended space missions.
details:
Eiserion — Complete Project Details

1. Project Overview

Eiserion is an AI-powered astronaut bone-health management system designed to address one of the major challenges of long-duration spaceflight: microgravity-induced bone loss.

The system integrates three main areas: bone-health monitoring, nutritional tracking, and exercise monitoring. By collecting and analyzing information from these areas, Eiserion aims to provide a more connected approach to astronaut health management.

Its central feature is an adaptive feedback system that connects nutritional intake with future exercise planning and exercise workload with future nutritional estimates. An AI component analyzes the collected information, identifies trends, explains recommendations, and highlights potential concerns or missing data.

The overall goal is to support skeletal health and more informed health management during extended space missions.

2. The Problem

In microgravity, astronauts experience significantly reduced mechanical loading on their bones. On Earth, gravity and everyday physical activities place continuous stress on the skeleton, stimulating normal bone remodeling.

In space, this mechanical stimulation is reduced. As a result, bone resorption can exceed bone formation, leading to gradual reductions in bone density and strength.

This can contribute to:

  • Reduced bone mineral density.
  • Decreased bone strength.
  • Increased fracture risk.
  • Changes in skeletal structure.
  • Extended recovery periods after returning to Earth.

The hip, pelvis, spine, and lower limbs are particularly important regions when studying spaceflight-related bone changes.

Although astronauts already follow nutritional and exercise countermeasures, combining different types of health information into an adaptive monitoring system remains a complex challenge.

3. Proposed Solution

Eiserion proposes an integrated platform that combines three main monitoring modules.

3.1 Bone-Health Monitoring

The bone-health module uses Quantitative Ultrasound (QUS) measurements to monitor changes in selected bone-related indicators.

The system is designed to record:

  • Speed of Sound (SOS).
  • Broadband Ultrasound Attenuation (BUA).
  • Measurement dates.
  • Anatomical measurement locations.
  • Measurement quality and reliability notes.
  • Historical measurement trends.

These measurements can help track changes in bone-related properties over time.

QUS is an indirect measurement technique. Its results depend on the measurement site and cannot independently establish total-body bone density or diagnose osteoporosis. Eiserion therefore treats QUS data as one component of a broader monitoring system.

3.2 Nutritional Monitoring

The nutrition module records daily nutritional intake and compares it with configured nutritional targets.

The system focuses on:

  • Total calorie intake.
  • Protein.
  • Carbohydrates.
  • Fat.
  • Calcium.
  • Vitamin D.
  • Vitamin C.
  • Magnesium.
  • Vitamin K.

The purpose is to monitor nutritional patterns and identify differences between recorded intake and configured targets.

Historical records can help the system identify recurring patterns rather than relying on individual daily measurements.

3.3 Exercise Monitoring

The exercise module records physical activity and exercise workload.

Information includes:

  • Exercise type.
  • Duration.
  • Intensity.
  • Resistance workload.
  • Sets and repetitions.
  • Exercise completion.
  • Historical activity records.

This information helps the system understand changes in physical workload and incorporate them into future planning.

4. Two-Way Adaptive Feedback System

One of Eiserion's central features is its two-way connection between nutrition and exercise.

Traditional tracking systems may treat nutritional intake and physical activity as separate categories. Eiserion proposes connecting them so that information from one module can influence future planning in the other.

The feedback system operates in two directions.

Nutrition to Exercise:

The system evaluates nutritional records and compares them with configured targets. This information can influence future exercise planning by highlighting nutritional considerations, incomplete records, or potential concerns.

Exercise to Nutrition:

The system evaluates exercise duration, intensity, and workload. This information can influence future nutritional estimates, particularly energy-planning calculations.

For example, if an astronaut records an increase in exercise workload, Eiserion can reassess its energy-planning estimates. Similarly, if nutritional records show that certain configured targets have not been reached, the system can consider this information when preparing future exercise suggestions.

The system continuously updates its analysis as new records become available.

These adjustments are intended as planning support, not medically validated prescriptions.

5. Artificial Intelligence Integration

Eiserion incorporates a locally running AI model to interpret collected information and communicate the system's findings.

The AI component is responsible for:

  • Analyzing nutritional and exercise records.
  • Explaining changes in estimated nutritional requirements.
  • Identifying patterns in historical data.
  • Interpreting changes in QUS measurements.
  • Explaining why a suggested plan has changed.
  • Highlighting missing or incomplete information.
  • Generating understandable summaries.
  • Providing context for system-generated suggestions.

The proposed model is Qwen 3.5 4B, running locally through Ollama.

An important architectural decision is separating calculations from AI interpretation.

Python handles numerical calculations, data processing, and predefined planning rules. The AI receives the resulting information and explains it to the user.

This reduces the risk of relying on a language model for scientific calculations and helps prevent invented measurements or unsupported numerical conclusions.

6. Scientific Foundation and Data Sources

Eiserion's scientific foundation draws on published research and information from international space agencies.

The main sources include:

NASA:

  • NASA Human Research Roadmap.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository.
  • NASA Life Sciences research resources.
  • NASA OCHMO Technical Brief on Food and Nutrition.
  • NASA research on astronaut bone loss, exercise, and nutritional requirements.

Canadian Space Agency:

  • TBone and TBone2 research projects.
  • Research examining changes in bone density, structure, and strength during long-duration spaceflight.
  • Studies using high-resolution peripheral quantitative computed tomography (HR-pQCT).

European Space Agency:

  • Research on vitamin K status and bone metabolism.
  • Head-down-tilt bed-rest studies investigating physiological changes associated with simulated microgravity.

These sources provide scientific background and reference data for the project's monitoring and analysis concepts.

It is important to distinguish between different measurement technologies. For example, the Canadian TBone studies used HR-pQCT, which is not interchangeable with QUS. Their findings can inform the project's scientific understanding, but their measurements cannot be directly entered as QUS values.

7. Application Structure

The proposed Eiserion application consists of seven main sections.

1. Dashboard

Provides an overview of the astronaut's recorded information, recent measurements, nutritional records, exercise activity, and relevant trends.

2. Astronaut Profile

Stores basic simulation parameters, including age, height, weight, activity information, and mission day.

3. Nutrition

Allows nutritional records to be entered, edited, reviewed, and compared with configured targets.

4. Exercise

Stores physical activity information, including exercise type, duration, intensity, workload, and completion.

5. Bone Health

Stores QUS measurements, measurement locations, dates, and historical SOS and BUA trends.

6. AI Analysis

Displays AI-generated explanations, identifies patterns, highlights missing information, and explains adaptive planning suggestions.

7. Settings

Provides data management, simulation configuration, and options for exporting or resetting demonstration records.

8. Technology Stack

The proposed prototype uses the following technologies:

  • Python: Main application logic, calculations, and adaptive planning.
  • Streamlit: Web-based application interface.
  • Pandas: Data organization and processing.
  • Plotly: Data visualization within the application.
  • JSON: Local data storage.
  • Ollama: Local AI model execution.
  • Qwen 3.5 4B: AI-based interpretation and explanations.

The prototype is designed to operate locally without requiring a cloud server.

9. System Workflow

The proposed workflow consists of six stages.

  1. Data Collection: Nutritional intake, exercise activity, and QUS measurements are entered or imported.
  2. Data Processing: Python organizes the information and checks for missing or incomplete records.
  3. Trend Analysis: The system compares current information with historical records.
  4. Adaptive Planning: Predefined rules use available nutritional and exercise information to adjust future estimates and suggestions.
  5. AI Interpretation: Qwen analyzes the processed information and explains the results.
  6. Continuous Monitoring: New records are added, allowing the system to follow changes throughout the mission.

10. Innovation and Key Features

Eiserion's main contribution is its proposed integration of several astronaut health-monitoring areas into one adaptive platform.

Its key features include:

  • Integration of bone-health, nutritional, and exercise information.
  • Two-way feedback between nutrition and exercise planning.
  • AI-generated explanations of system results.
  • Historical tracking of bone-related measurements.
  • Identification of missing information and potential concerns.
  • Local AI processing.
  • Modular architecture that could support additional sensors and data sources in future versions.

Rather than treating nutritional intake, exercise, and bone health as isolated subjects, Eiserion explores how information from these areas can be considered together.

11. Limitations and Future Development

The initial version of Eiserion is a research and demonstration prototype.

Its current development focuses on manually entered or simulated data, predefined planning rules, QUS record management, and AI-generated explanations.

Future development could include:

  • Direct integration with QUS measurement hardware.
  • Automatic collection of nutritional information.
  • Integration with exercise equipment and activity sensors.
  • Additional physiological monitoring.
  • More advanced personalized planning algorithms.
  • Integration with established astronaut health-monitoring systems.
  • Validation using appropriate clinical and spaceflight research data.

Before operational use in spaceflight, the system would require extensive scientific validation, reliable hardware integration, medical oversight, and testing under relevant mission conditions.

Eiserion is not intended to replace existing NASA health systems or medical professionals.

12. Expected Impact

Eiserion aims to support astronaut health management during long-duration missions by connecting information that is often monitored through different systems.

Its expected contributions include:

  • Improved visibility of bone-health trends.
  • More connected nutritional and exercise monitoring.
  • Better understanding of relationships between physical workload and nutritional intake.
  • Adaptive planning based on recorded information.
  • Clearer explanations of health-related data.
  • A foundation for future integrated astronaut health-management technologies.

13. Project Mission

The mission of Eiserion is to explore how artificial intelligence, bone-health measurements, nutritional monitoring, and exercise data can be integrated into one adaptive system to support skeletal health during long-duration spaceflight.

Eiserion aims to help protect astronaut bone health by connecting monitoring, analysis, and adaptive planning into a unified platform.
